def-gmm-gee.title: Generalized estimating equations
def-gmm-gee.html:
Let V be a variance function and ϕ a dispersion, and write 𝛃𝛃𝛍𝛃AiV(β)=diag{V(μi1),…,V(μini)},Di(β)=∂μi∂β⊤=diag{h′(ηij)}Xi. Let 𝛂Ri(α) be a working correlation matrix: a correlation matrix for the ni observations of cluster i, depending on a finite parameter 𝛂α, chosen by the analyst and not assumed correct. The working covariance is 𝛃𝛂𝛂Vi(β,α,ϕ)=ϕ(AiV)1/2Ri(α)(AiV)1/2,{#eq-gmm-working-covariance}

and the generalized estimating equation is 𝛃𝛂𝛃𝛍𝛃Um(β;α,ϕ)=∑i=1mDi(β)⊤Vi−1{Yi−μi(β)}=0.{#eq-gmm-gee}

In practice 𝛂α and ϕ are replaced by moment estimates computed from the Pearson residuals rij=(yij−μ^ij)/V(μ^ij) at the current 𝛃β^, and @eq-gmm-gee is re-solved, until nothing changes.

def-gmm-glmm.title: Generalized linear mixed model
def-gmm-glmm.html:
Let 𝛉u∼Nq{0,G(θ)} be a vector of random effects with covariance depending on unknown variance components 𝛉θ. Given u, let the responses Y1,…,Yn be independent, each from the exponential dispersion family @def-glm-edf with prior weight wi, dispersion ϕ and variance function V, and with conditional mean 𝛃μi(u)=E(Yi∣u)=h(ηi),ηi=x(i)⊤β+z(i)⊤u,{#eq-gmm-model}

so that Var(Yi∣u)=ϕV{μi(u)}/wi. In matrix form 𝛈𝛃η=Xβ+Zu with X of size n×p and Z of size n×q, both known. The parameters are the fixed effects 𝛃β, the variance components 𝛉θ and, if it is not fixed by the family, the dispersion ϕ.

exm-gmm-attenuation.title: Attenuation in a logistic random-intercept model
exm-gmm-attenuation.title_html: Attenuation in a logistic random-intercept model
exm-gmm-attenuation.html: Take α=0, βC=1 and a covariate X∼N(0,1), and solve @eq-gmm-marginal-parameter numerically. With τ=0.5 the marginal slope is 0.9502; with τ=1 it is 0.8379; with τ=2 it is 0.6142. The approximation @eq-gmm-logit-factor gives 0.8620 and 0.6477 in the last two cases, too large by about three and five per cent. The probit factor at τ=1 is 0.7071, far smaller — but that is a different model, with a different meaning for βC. The covariate distribution matters little: at τ=1 a binary covariate gives a marginal log odds ratio of 0.8318. Figure 40.1.1(a) shows why the approximation works at all — the average of the conditional curves is almost exactly a flatter logistic curve — and panel (b) tracks βM/βC as the clusters become more heterogeneous.

exm-gmm-compare.title: Three methods on clustered binary data
exm-gmm-compare.title_html: Three methods on clustered binary data
exm-gmm-compare.html:
Simulate 150 clusters of 5 binary observations from a random-intercept logistic model with 𝛃β=(−0.5,1.0)⊤, a covariate varying within the cluster, and τ=1. Over 200 replications the average estimates are

β^1 (truth 1.0) τ^ (truth 1.0)
PQL 0.8970 0.8168
Laplace 1.0022 0.9353
adaptive Gauss–Hermite, K=9 1.0087 0.9909

PQL attenuates the slope by 10.3 per cent and the standard deviation by 18.3 per cent. The Laplace approximation is nearly unbiased for the slope but still shrinks τ^ by about six per cent, which is consistent with the O(ni−1) error of @thm-gmm-likelihood(b) at ni=5; the direction and size of the induced bias are measured here, not derived, since part (b) bounds the error in the likelihood and says nothing about where its maximizer moves. Nine adaptive nodes leave a bias of about one per cent, which is the ordinary finite-sample bias of maximum likelihood rather than a numerical error.

Panel (c) of Figure 40.3.1 separates the numerical question from the statistical one. At a fixed parameter value, the error in the integrated log-likelihood with K=5 is 3.65136×10−3 for the adaptive rule and 1.01404×10−1 for the plain one — a factor of about 28 — and the adaptive rule is down to 3.759×10−10 by K=13, while the plain one is still above 10−6, at 2.460×10−6, when K=19.

exm-gmm-coverage.title: Coverage when the working correlation is wrong
exm-gmm-coverage.title_html: Coverage when the working correlation is wrong
exm-gmm-coverage.html:
Generate clusters of ni=8 binary responses from a random-intercept logistic model with τ=1.5, one covariate varying within the cluster and one fixed for the whole cluster (a treatment assigned to clusters), and fit the marginal model by GEE with an independence working correlation — wrong by construction. The target is the marginal cluster-level coefficient, which @eq-gmm-marginal-parameter puts at 0.5748 when the conditional coefficient is 0.8. Over 600 replications at m=240 the mean estimate is 0.5681: consistent for the marginal coefficient, and not for the conditional one.

The three intervals behave quite differently. The model-based interval covers 0.757 of the time and does not improve with m: it is wrong, not merely imprecise. The sandwich covers 0.913 at m=15 and 0.947 at m=240, and the bias-corrected sandwich with a t reference covers 0.973 at m=15 — slightly conservative, which at that sample size is the right side to err on.

exm-gmm-efficiency.title: How much efficiency is at stake
exm-gmm-efficiency.title_html: How much efficiency is at stake
exm-gmm-efficiency.html:
Simulate 60 clusters of 6 Poisson counts with a log link, one covariate varying within the cluster and one constant within it, and generate the dependence in two ways: a shared random intercept, which makes the true correlation exchangeable, and a latent Gaussian AR(1) process with ρ=0.8. Fit by GEE with each of the four working correlations and record the sampling variance of each coefficient over 400 replications.

For the within-cluster covariate under exchangeable truth, the efficiency of the exchangeable working correlation relative to independence is 1.789; AR(1) and unstructured reach 1.583 and 1.547. Under AR(1) truth the figures are 1.282 for AR(1), 1.183 for exchangeable and 1.160 for unstructured. Matching the truth helps, mismatching it still helps, and the gain is worth having without being dramatic.

For the cluster-level covariate the ranking reverses: under exchangeable truth the relative efficiencies are 0.889, 0.938 and 0.834, all below one, so independence is best of the four. The reason is @exr-gmm-two-clusters: a covariate constant within a cluster is estimated from cluster means, on which an exchangeable reweighting has no effect at all, so all a nontrivial Ri contributes is the noise in 𝛂α^.

exm-gmm-grunfeld.title: Grunfeld’s firms, again
exm-gmm-grunfeld.html:
Chapter 32 fitted a linear mixed model to Grunfeld’s panel of 11 US firms observed in each of 20 years (@exm-mix-grunfeld). Investment there ranges over three orders of magnitude and is far more variable for large firms than for small ones, which a constant-variance model cannot represent; a gamma response with a log link can, because the mean is multiplicative and the conditional coefficient of variation is constant. With Yij the gross investment of firm i in year j, Yij∣ui∼Gamma withlog⁡E(Yij∣ui)=β0+β1log⁡(valueij)+β2log⁡(capitalij)+ui, ui∼N(0,τ2), and Var(Yij∣ui)=ϕE(Yij∣ui)2. Fitting by adaptive Gauss–Hermite quadrature (Section 40.3) gives

β1 (value) β2 (capital) ϕ τ
marginal gamma GLM 0.8421 0.3386 0.2644 —
gamma GLMM 0.6825 0.2315 0.0930 0.5188

The firm-to-firm standard deviation τ^=0.5188 is large: firms a standard deviation apart on the log scale differ by a factor of e0.5188≈1.68 in investment at the same value and capital stock. The conditional coefficient of variation is ϕ^=0.3049. For a gamma with shape 1/ϕ^ the conditional variance of log⁡Y is the trigamma function of the shape, 0.0974, so the fraction of the variance of log⁡Y attributable to the firm is τ^2/(τ^2+0.0974)=0.734.

The fitted conditional intercept is −1.3032; by @prp-gmm-marginal(b) the log link causes no attenuation of the slopes, and the marginal intercept is −1.3032+τ^2/2=−1.1686. The difference between the two rows is therefore not the marginal–conditional distinction. It is the older within-versus-between problem of Section 6.6: the independence fit lets differences between firms contribute to the slopes, while the mixed model assigns most of them to ui and estimates the slopes mainly from movement within a firm. A gap of this size accuses the mean model, and Section 40.5 returns to it with a diagnostic and two candidate explanations, @exr-gmm-within-between with a remedy.

exm-gmm-modechoice.title: Four options per traveller
exm-gmm-modechoice.html:
Each of 210 travellers between Australian cities chose one of four modes — air, train, bus, car — and the data record, for every traveller and every mode, the terminal waiting time and a generalized cost. Take Yij=1 if traveller i chose mode j, fit a logistic model with mode indicators, waiting time and cost, and treat each traveller as a cluster of ni=4. The sample deliberately over-represents the rarer modes, so by @thm-bin-casecontrol the mode indicators and the intercept are shifted by the sampling design and are not population quantities; the within-traveller coefficients are unaffected, and standard errors are the point here in any case.

The four records of a traveller are anything but independent: exactly one is a 1. An independence working correlation gives the same coefficients as ordinary logistic regression, so the question is only what the standard errors should be. The ratio of the sandwich standard error to the model-based one ranges from 0.694 to 1.558 across the six coefficients: for terminal waiting time, whose coefficient is −1.0693 per ten minutes, the sandwich standard error is 1.558 times larger (0.1698 against 0.1090); for generalized cost, whose coefficient is −0.0098 per ten dollars, it is 0.694 times as large (0.0138 against 0.0199).

The sandwich is not a device for making standard errors bigger. Negative within-cluster correlation makes within-cluster contrasts better determined than independence would suggest, and cost is such a contrast; waiting time is confounded with the mode indicators, which the traveller’s single choice constrains, and is therefore worse determined. Two further observations. The Pearson dispersion estimate is 5.155, which looks like extreme overdispersion and means nothing: Bernoulli responses carry no information about a dispersion parameter (@prp-gmm-moments(b) with Ni=1). And the exchangeable working correlation estimate is −0.3015, close to the smallest value −1/(ni−1)=−1/3 an exchangeable matrix of size four can have: there the smallest eigenvalue of R is 1+3α^=0.0956. An almost singular structure is a bad working covariance, and independence is the sensible choice.

exm-gmm-poisson-lognormal.title: The Poisson–lognormal model
exm-gmm-poisson-lognormal.html: With Yi∣ui Poisson (@def-cnt-poisson) of mean 𝛃exp⁡(x(i)⊤β+ui) and ui∼N(0,τ2), the conditional mean is multiplied by the lognormal variable eui. Unlike the binary case this model is identified with a single observation per unit, because the Poisson variance is determined by its mean and any excess must come from ui: it is an overdispersion model in the sense of Chapter 38 (@prp-ql-overdispersion), and a direct competitor to the negative binomial of @def-cnt-negbin, which arises the same way with a gamma mixing variable (@lem-cnt-gamma-mixture).

exm-gmm-qic.title: Grunfeld’s panel by GEE
exm-gmm-qic.html:
Fit the marginal version of @exm-gmm-grunfeld — gamma variance function V(μ)=μ2, log link, investment on log value and log capital — to the 11 firms by GEE. The AR(1) working correlation estimates a lag-one correlation of 0.894, as one expects of annual investment figures. Yet QIC, with the dispersion held at the independence estimate of the larger model, ranks the four structures

Structure QIC, value and capital QIC, value only
independence 8450.1 8657.6
exchangeable 8524.2 8647.4
AR(1) 8574.1 8657.8
unstructured 8754.7 8704.1

and prefers independence. As a comparison of mean models the table is informative: at three of the four structures the model with capital wins, by between about 80 and 210 QIC units, and that is the comparison QIC was designed for. Under the unstructured correlation the ranking reverses, which with 11 clusters and a 20×20 matrix to estimate is a comment on the structure rather than on the model. As a comparison of structures the column mostly reports that the sandwich is smallest under independence — the remark above in numerical form.

The estimates themselves are the more interesting output. The independence fit gives β^value=0.8421 and β^capital=0.3386; the exchangeable fit gives 0.7214 and 0.2113. The gap in the first coefficient is more than its sandwich standard error of 0.1030, and the two gaps point the same way. By @thm-gmm-gee(a) that accuses the mean model, and two standard explanations fit equally well: firm effects correlated with the covariates, as @exm-gmm-grunfeld found, or feedback from investment to the following years’ market value, which violates the full-covariate conditional mean condition and makes the exchangeable fit — not the independence one — the inconsistent member of the pair. Either way the remedy is to separate the two sources of variation. Adding the firm means of log value and log capital, as @exr-gmm-within-between asks, makes the independence and exchangeable estimates agree to machine precision, at within-firm slopes 0.6142 and 0.2298, both well below the independence figures above.

exm-gmm-random-intercept-logit.title: A random-intercept logistic model
exm-gmm-random-intercept-logit.html: m physicians each treat ni patients; Yij=1 if patient j of physician i recovers. With the logistic link of @def-bin-logistic, 𝛃logitPr(Yij=1∣ui)=x(ij)⊤β+ui and ui∼N(0,τ2), the coefficient of a patient-level covariate compares two patients of the same physician, and τ measures how much physicians differ. A useful summary is the median odds ratio exp⁡(2τz0.75), the median odds ratio between two randomly chosen physicians treating identical patients (@exr-gmm-mor). Replacing ui by u0i+u1ixij gives a random-slope model, at the price of three parameters in G0 and, by @exr-gmm-probit-general, no single marginal coefficient at all.

exr-gmm-attenuation-bound.title: B1
exr-gmm-attenuation-bound.html: Use @eq-gmm-attenuation-derivative to show that in a logistic random-intercept model with Pr(Y=1∣U)=h(U) and U symmetric about 0, the attenuation factor at θ=0 equals 1−4Var{h(U)}. Evaluate it for U∼N(0,1), for which Var{h(U)}=0.0434, and compare with the ratio 0.8379 of @exm-gmm-attenuation.

exr-gmm-effective-n.title: B2
exr-gmm-effective-n.html: For a cluster of n Bernoulli responses with common success probability π and a random intercept, show that ci=nπ(1−π)+τ−2. Compare with the gamma case of @exm-gmm-grunfeld, where ci=n/ϕ+τ−2, and use @thm-gmm-likelihood(b) to explain the difference between the two fits in terms of an effective cluster size.

exr-gmm-efficiency-bound.title: C1
exr-gmm-efficiency-bound.html: Show that if Vi=Σi0 then A−1BA−1=A−1 is the smallest asymptotic covariance attainable in the class of @exr-gmm-unbiased-family, in the nonnegative-definite ordering. (Hint: for any Gi, compare (∑Gi⊤Di)−1(∑Gi⊤Σi0Gi)(∑Di⊤Gi)−1 with A−1 using a Cauchy–Schwarz argument in the inner product ⟨a,b⟩=∑iai⊤Σi0bi.)

exr-gmm-exchangeable-bound.title: B1
exr-gmm-exchangeable-bound.html: Show that the exchangeable correlation matrix R=(1−α)I+α11⊤ of size n has eigenvalues 1+(n−1)α (once) and 1−α (n−1 times), so that it is positive definite exactly when −1/(n−1)<α<1. Verify the value 1+3α^=0.0956 quoted in @exm-gmm-modechoice from α^=−0.3015, and say what a practitioner should do when a moment estimate falls outside the range.

exr-gmm-hausman.title: B2
exr-gmm-hausman.html: Formalize the diagnostic of @exm-gmm-qic. Let 𝛃β^I and 𝛃β^E be the independence and exchangeable GEE estimates. Explain why 𝛃𝛃β^I−β^E has mean zero to first order when the mean model is correct, and why its covariance is not the difference of the two covariances in general. What resampling scheme would give a usable reference distribution?

exr-gmm-identify.title: A1
exr-gmm-identify.html: For each of the following, say whether the random-intercept variance τ2 is identified, and why: (a) one Bernoulli response per cluster; (b) one binomial response with Ni=40 trials per cluster; (c) one Poisson count per cluster; (d) five Bernoulli responses per cluster.

exr-gmm-independence-same.title: A1
exr-gmm-independence-same.html: Show from @eq-gmm-gee that with Ri=I the estimate 𝛃β^ does not depend on ϕ or on the cluster structure at all, and equals the ordinary generalized linear model estimate. Which quantities do depend on the clustering?

exr-gmm-kappa.title: A2
exr-gmm-kappa.html: A Poisson–lognormal model is fitted and gives τ^2=0.5. What NB2 shape parameter κ would produce the same marginal variance function? Would you expect the two models to give noticeably different fitted means?

exr-gmm-log-link-check.title: A2
exr-gmm-log-link-check.html: A Poisson random-intercept model with a log link is fitted and reports α^=−1.2, β^=0.35, τ^2=0.8. What does a population-averaged log-linear model estimate? Which of the three numbers changes?

exr-gmm-mor.title: B1
exr-gmm-mor.html: In @exm-gmm-random-intercept-logit, let two physicians be drawn at random and let OR be the odds ratio between them for identical patients, taken in the direction that makes it at least one. Show that the median of OR is exp⁡(2τz0.75), where z0.75=0.6745 is the upper quartile of the standard normal. Evaluate it for τ=1.

exr-gmm-negative.title: B2
exr-gmm-negative.html: Give a two-level model with a vector random effect whose induced within-cluster correlation is negative, and explain why @lem-gmm-association does not apply. (Hint: let z(ij) differ in sign across j.)

exr-gmm-nodes.title: A1
exr-gmm-nodes.html: A GLMM with two correlated random effects per cluster is fitted by non-adaptive Gauss–Hermite quadrature on a product grid. How many likelihood evaluations per cluster does K=20 cost? What if there are four random effects per cluster? What does this say about crossed random effects, where q0 is effectively the whole vector?

exr-gmm-one-node.title: B1
exr-gmm-one-node.html: Verify @thm-gmm-likelihood(c) for K=1 directly: show that the one-point Gauss–Hermite rule has node z1=0 and weight w1=π, and that @eq-gmm-aghq then reduces to @eq-gmm-laplace without its correction terms. Then explain why the non-adaptive rule with K=1 gives something quite different, and say what.

exr-gmm-probit-general.title: B2
exr-gmm-probit-general.html: Extend @prp-gmm-marginal(c) to a probit model with a random slope: Pr(Y=1∣U0,U1)=Φ(α+βx+U0+U1x) with (U0,U1)∼N2(0,G). Show that the marginal curve is Φ{(α+βx)/s(x)} with s(x)2=1+(1,x)G(1,x)⊤, and explain why the marginal model is now not a probit model in x at all.

exr-gmm-qic-reading.title: A2
exr-gmm-qic-reading.html: In @exm-gmm-qic, QIC prefers independence among the working correlations but the AR(1) parameter is estimated at 0.894. Are these two statements in conflict? Explain what each of them is measuring.

exr-gmm-two-clusters.title: B1
exr-gmm-two-clusters.html: Take m clusters of size 2, the identity link, V≡1, ϕ=1, and an exchangeable working correlation with parameter α. Show that @eq-gmm-gee reduces to weighted least squares with weight matrix R−1, R=(1−α)I+αJ, in each cluster, and that when x(i1)=x(i2) for every i the estimate does not depend on α at all. Interpret.

exr-gmm-two-targets.title: A1
exr-gmm-two-targets.html: A random-intercept logistic model for whether a pupil passes an examination has β^C=0.60 for one extra hour of study per week and τ^=1.2. Use @eq-gmm-logit-factor to say roughly what a population-averaged logistic model would report, and state in one sentence each what the two numbers mean.

exr-gmm-unbiased-family.title: B2
exr-gmm-unbiased-family.html: Let Gi be any ni×p matrix depending on 𝛃β but not on Yi. Show that 𝛍∑iGi⊤(Yi−μi) is an unbiased estimating function and that @eq-gmm-gee is the member with Gi=Vi−1Di. Which member is optimal, in the sense of @prp-ql-optimality, and why is it not available?

exr-gmm-what-target.title: A2
exr-gmm-what-target.html: A trial randomizes clinics to a new protocol and measures a binary outcome on patients within clinics. The investigators want to report “the effect of the protocol on a patient’s odds of recovery”. Which method should they use, and what would a GEE analysis report instead?

exr-gmm-which-method.title: A2
exr-gmm-which-method.html: For each of the following, say whether PQL is likely to be adequate and why: (a) counts with means in the hundreds, ten per cluster; (b) binary responses, three per cluster, with a large estimated τ; (c) grouped binomial responses with Ni=200 trials, one per cluster.

exr-gmm-which-structure.title: A1
exr-gmm-which-structure.html: For each design, name the working correlation you would use and say why: (a) pupils within 300 schools, class size varying; (b) five annual measurements on each of 500 patients; (c) left and right eyes of 80 patients; (d) irregularly timed clinic visits, between two and eleven per patient, 1200 patients.

exr-gmm-within-between.title: C1
exr-gmm-within-between.html: In @exm-gmm-grunfeld the mixed-model slopes differ markedly from the independence ones. Add the firm means log⁡value―i and log⁡capital―i to the model as extra fixed effects, so that the original covariates carry only within-firm variation. Explain why this makes the random effect orthogonal to the covariates in the population, refit, and compare. What test does the difference between the two specifications suggest?

lem-gmm-association.title: A shared random intercept induces nonnegative correlation
lem-gmm-association.title_html: A shared random intercept induces nonnegative correlation
lem-gmm-association.html: Let U be a random variable and f,g:R→R both nondecreasing, with Ef(U)2 and Eg(U)2 finite. Then Cov{f(U),g(U)}≥0. Consequently, in a random-intercept GLMM @eq-gmm-random-intercept-model with any inverse link h that is nondecreasing, Cov(Yij,Yik)=Cov{h(ηij0+ui),h(ηik0+ui)}≥0(j≠k).

prp-gmm-marginal.title: Marginal and conditional coefficients
prp-gmm-marginal.html:
Let U have mean zero and let h be the inverse link of the model @eq-gmm-random-intercept.

  1. Identity link. If h(η)=η then m(x)=α+βx, so αM=α and βM=β for every distribution of U with mean zero. The two targets coincide.

  2. Log link. If h(η)=eη and EeU<∞, then m(x)=E(eU)eα+βx, so βM=β and αM=α+log⁡EeU. For U∼N(0,τ2) the shift is τ2/2. Only the intercept moves.

  3. Probit link. If h=Φ and U∼N(0,τ2) then m(x)=Φ(α+βx1+τ2),{#eq-gmm-probit-exact}

    so the marginal mean function is again a probit, with αM=α/1+τ2 and βM=β/1+τ2.

  4. Logit link. Let h(η)=eη/(1+eη), let U be any random variable with 0<Var{h(θ+U)}<∞ for every θ, and put Pθ=h(θ+U) and F(θ)=g{EPθ}, the marginal linear predictor. Then F′(θ)=1−Var(Pθ)E(Pθ)E(1−Pθ)∈(0,1).{#eq-gmm-attenuation-derivative}

    Consequently, if β≠0, then for any x1<x2 the marginal log odds ratio is strictly attenuated: 0<sign(β){gm(x2)−gm(x1)}<|β|(x2−x1). In particular a binary covariate has 0<|βM|<|βC|.

prp-gmm-moments.title: Marginal moments of a GLMM
prp-gmm-moments.html:
In @def-gmm-glmm write μi(u)=h(ηi) and μiM=E{μi(u)}.

  1. E(Yi)=μiM, Var(Yi)=ϕwiE[V{μi(u)}]+Var{μi(u)},{#eq-gmm-marginal-variance}

    and Cov(Yi,Yk)=Cov{μi(u),μk(u)} for i≠k. The marginal variance always exceeds the average conditional variance.

  2. Binomial. If Yi∣u∼Bin{Ni,πi(u)} and π¯i=Eπi(u), then E(Yi)=Niπ¯i and Var(Yi)=Niπ¯i(1−π¯i){1+(Ni−1)Var{πi(u)}π¯i(1−π¯i)}.{#eq-gmm-binomial-overdispersion}

    The overdispersion factor is the beta-binomial one, and it equals 1 when Ni=1: a single Bernoulli response carries no trace of the random effect.

  3. Poisson with a log link, ϕ=1, and a random intercept ui∼N(0,τ2) shared by the observations of a cluster. Then 𝛃μijM=exp⁡(x(ij)⊤β+τ2/2), Var(Yij)=μijM+(μijM)2(eτ2−1),Cov(Yij,Yik)=μijMμikM(eτ2−1).{#eq-gmm-poisson-moments}

    The marginal variance function is exactly the NB2 function V(μ)=μ+μ2/κ of @def-cnt-negbin, with κ=1/(eτ2−1) — although the marginal distribution is not negative binomial and has no closed form.

prp-gmm-pql.title: Penalized quasi-likelihood
prp-gmm-pql.html:
In @def-gmm-glmm let 𝛃ℓ(β,u) be the conditional log-likelihood of the data given u, and consider the penalized quasi-likelihood 𝛃𝛃ℓpen(β,u)=ℓ(β,u)−12u⊤G−1u.{#eq-gmm-pql-objective}

  1. For fixed 𝛉θ, the stationary equations of @eq-gmm-pql-objective are 𝛍𝛍X⊤WD−1(y−μ)=0,Z⊤WD−1(y−μ)=ϕG−1u, with W and D the working weights and derivatives of @thm-glm-score evaluated at 𝛈𝛃η=Xβ+Zu. Equivalently, with the working response 𝛈𝛍z=η+D−1(y−μ) of @eq-glm-working-response, they are Henderson’s mixed-model equations (@thm-mix-henderson) for the linear mixed model 𝛃z∣u∼Nn(Xβ+Zu, ϕW−1), u∼Nq(0,G).

  2. Iterating — update 𝛃(β,u) by those equations, then update 𝛉θ by maximum likelihood or REML in the working linear mixed model, and repeat — is the Breslow–Clayton PQL algorithm. It is therefore the Laplace approximation @eq-gmm-laplace with the further simplification that W is treated as fixed when 𝛉θ is updated, so that ci contributes no derivative terms.

  3. The resulting 𝛃β^ and 𝛉θ^ are biased towards zero, and the bias does not vanish as m→∞ with cluster sizes fixed: PQL is inconsistent. It is worst for binary responses with small ni and large τ, and negligible for responses that carry much information per observation.

prp-gmm-prediction.title: Empirical Bayes prediction and shrinkage
prp-gmm-prediction.html:
Consider @eq-gmm-random-intercept-model with 𝛃β, τ2 and ϕ known, write ℓi(u)=∑jlog⁡f(yij∣u) for cluster i’s conditional log-likelihood, and assume ℓi is concave in u — as it is for a canonical link by @thm-glm-concave, and for the gamma with a log link by direct differentiation.

  1. The posterior density of ui given yi, proportional to exp⁡{ℓi(u)−u2/(2τ2)}, is log-concave and its mode u^i is unique.

  2. If ℓi attains its maximum at a finite a^i≠0, then u^i lies strictly between 0 and a^i: the prediction has the same sign as the cluster’s own estimate and is strictly smaller in magnitude. If ℓi has no finite maximizer — as when every response in a binary cluster is 0 — then u^i is finite all the same.

  3. Replacing ℓi by its quadratic expansion at a^i gives u^i≈{τ2/(τ2+Ii−1)}a^i with Ii=−ℓi″(a^i). In the two cases used in this chapter Ii−1=ϕ/ni exactly, which is @eq-mix-shrinkage: clusters with few observations are shrunk harder, and all clusters are shrunk harder when τ2 is small relative to the noise.

prp-gmm-working.title: Choosing the working correlation
prp-gmm-working.html:
In the setting of @thm-gmm-gee:

  1. Efficiency. The asymptotic covariance A−1BA−1 of @eq-gmm-gee-asymptotics is minimized, in the nonnegative-definite ordering and over all unbiased estimating functions linear in 𝛍Yi−μi, by Vi=Σi0 (@exr-gmm-efficiency-bound). Any other working covariance costs efficiency, but the cost depends on the covariate: it is substantial for a covariate that varies within clusters and negligible for one that is constant within a cluster, for which the independence choice is in fact hard to beat.

  2. Small samples. The sandwich @eq-gmm-sandwich is biased downwards by a term of order p/m, so Wald tests built on it reject too often when m is small; the bias-corrected forms of Section 40.4 and a tm−p reference repair most of it. The bias grows with the number of parameters in Ri, because 𝛂α^ is then noisier and condition (E5) of @thm-gmm-gee is stretched.

  3. QIC. Since there is no likelihood, AIC is unavailable. Pan’s quasi-likelihood information criterion replaces the log-likelihood by the quasi-likelihood 𝛍Q(μ;y)=∑ij∫yijμij(yij−t)/{ϕV(t)}dt of @def-ql-quasi computed under the independence working correlation at the fitted 𝛍μ^, with ϕ the Pearson estimate of @prp-ql-dispersion held fixed across the models compared, and replaces the parameter count by a sandwich-based trace: 𝛍QIC=−2Q(μ^;y)+2tr(Ω^IV^R),{#eq-gmm-qic}

    where Ω^I=∑iD^i⊤(A^iV)−1D^i/ϕ is the independence-model information and V^R is @eq-gmm-sandwich. If the working model is correct the trace is p and @eq-gmm-qic is the Akaike form @def-sel-aic-bic. It is a sound criterion for choosing the mean model, and a weakly justified one for choosing Ri.

thm-gmm-gee.title: Consistency, asymptotic normality and the sandwich
thm-gmm-gee.title_html: Consistency, asymptotic normality and the sandwich
thm-gmm-gee.html:
Let the clusters be independent, let 𝛃β0 be the true value in @eq-gmm-gee-mean, and let Σi0=Cov(Yi) be arbitrary and unknown. Assume

  • (E1) ni≤nmax and ‖x(ij)‖≤C for all i,j;
  • (E2) h is twice continuously differentiable with h′ bounded, V is continuous and bounded away from 0 on the relevant range, and 𝛃β0 is interior to a compact parameter set;
  • (E3) the eigenvalues of 𝛂Ri(α) are bounded above and away from zero, uniformly in i and in 𝛂α near its limit;
  • (E4) E‖Yi‖4≤K for all i;
  • (E5) 𝛂α^ and ϕ^ are m-consistent for some limits 𝛂α∗,ϕ∗, which need not make Vi equal to Σi0;
  • (E6) with Vi evaluated at 𝛃𝛂(β0,α∗,ϕ∗), Am=1m∑iDi⊤Vi−1Di→A,Bm=1m∑iDi⊤Vi−1Σi0Vi−1Di→B, both positive definite.

Then:

  1. Unbiasedness. For every fixed 𝛂α and ϕ, 𝛃𝛂E{Um(β0;α,ϕ)}=0. The estimating function is unbiased whatever the working correlation is.

  2. Consistency and asymptotic normality. With probability tending to one, @eq-gmm-gee has a root 𝛃β^m with 𝛃𝛃β^m→β0 in probability, and 𝛃𝛃m(β^m−β0) →d Np(0, A−1BA−1).{#eq-gmm-gee-asymptotics}

  3. The sandwich estimator. Let 𝛍𝛃ri=Yi−μi(β^m) and V^R=A^m−1(∑iD^i⊤V^i−1riri⊤V^i−1D^i)A^m−1,A^m=∑iD^i⊤V^i−1D^i,{#eq-gmm-sandwich}

    with hats denoting evaluation at 𝛃𝛂β^m,α^,ϕ^; A^m is m times the sample version of the Am of (E6). Then mV^R→A−1BA−1 in probability, and the Wald statistic of a hypothesis 𝛃Λ⊤β of rank q, formed with V^R, tends to χ2(q).

  4. When the model-based covariance is valid. If the working covariance is correct, Vi=Σi0, then B=A and @eq-gmm-gee-asymptotics reduces to A−1, which the model-based estimator V^M=(∑iD^i⊤V^i−1D^i)−1 estimates consistently. Otherwise V^M is inconsistent, in either direction.

thm-gmm-likelihood.title: The integrated likelihood and its approximations
thm-gmm-likelihood.title_html: The integrated likelihood and its approximations
thm-gmm-likelihood.html:
In @def-gmm-glmm write 𝛃𝛉ψi(ui)=log⁡f(yi∣ui;β,ϕ)+log⁡p(ui;θ).

  1. Factorization. If the random effects split into independent blocks u1,…,um with ui entering only the observations of cluster i, then 𝛃𝛉L(β,θ,ϕ)=∏i=1m∫Rq0exp⁡{ψi(ui)}dui,{#eq-gmm-factorized}

    a product of m integrals of dimension q0.

  2. Laplace approximation. Fix i and take q0=1. Let ψi be four times continuously differentiable with a unique interior maximizer u^i, and ci=−ψi″(u^i)>0. Then, formally, ∫eψi(u)du=2πcieψi(u^i){1+δi+…},δi=ψi(4)(u^i)8ci2+5{ψi‴(u^i)}224ci3.{#eq-gmm-laplace}

    Suppose ψi=niki+si, where ki does not depend on ni and has a nondegenerate maximum and si has derivatives bounded uniformly in ni. (In a GLMM niki is the conditional log-likelihood and si the log prior density of ui, which does not grow with ni.) Then both terms of δi are O(ni−1): the Laplace approximation has relative error O(ni−1) and the error in the log-likelihood is O(∑ini−1).

  3. Adaptive Gauss–Hermite quadrature. Let (zk,wk)k=1K be the nodes and weights of K-point Gauss–Hermite quadrature, so that ∫e−z2P(z)dz=∑kwkP(zk) for every polynomial P of degree at most 2K−1. With σ^i=ci−1/2, the substitution u=u^i+2σ^iz gives the approximation ∫eψi(u)du≈2σ^i∑k=1Kwkezk2eψi(u^i+2σ^izk).{#eq-gmm-aghq}

    It is exact whenever eψi(u^i+2σ^iz)+z2 is a polynomial of degree at most 2K−1 in z, and K=1 reproduces @eq-gmm-laplace without its correction terms.

  4. Penalized quasi-likelihood avoids the integral altogether, by a penalized maximization that is cheaper than either of the above and carries a bias that does not vanish. It is stated and proved separately as @prp-gmm-pql.
